recipes.title: New Orleans Muffuletta with Olive Salad
recipes.blurb: A round sesame loaf packed with cured meats, provolone, and a briny olive salad, then pressed for hours until the oil soaks through. Built the night before, which is the whole idea.

items: 1 cup (150 g) pitted green olives, roughly chopped
¾ cup (110 g) pitted Kalamata olives, roughly chopped
1 cup (200 g) giardiniera, drained and chopped
½ cup (120 ml) extra-virgin olive oil
½ tsp (1 g) coarsely ground black pepper
1 round sesame-topped muffuletta or Italian loaf, 10 in (25 cm) across
6 oz (170 g) thinly sliced Genoa salami
6 oz (170 g) thinly sliced capicola or deli ham

instructions.title: Make the olive salad first
instructions.text: Combine the chopped green and Kalamata olives, giardiniera, capers, minced garlic, parsley, oregano, olive oil, red wine vinegar, and pepper in a bowl and stir well. Do not add salt — between the olives, capers, and giardiniera there is plenty already. You should have about 3 cups (700 ml).

instructions.title: Let it marinate a full day
instructions.text: Cover the olive salad and refrigerate at least 24 hours, and up to a week if you can plan that far ahead. This rest is not optional: it lets the garlic mellow, the oregano bloom in the oil, and all the briny flavors merge into one thing rather than a bowl of separate chopped items. Stir it once before you use it.

instructions.title: Split the loaf
instructions.text: Slice the round loaf in half horizontally with a long serrated knife, sawing gently and keeping the blade level so you get two even halves. The bread should be soft-crumbed with a thin sesame crust — sturdy enough to hold up, soft enough to compress. A crusty sourdough boule is the wrong choice and will fight you at every bite.

instructions.title: Hollow the top half
instructions.text: Pull out some of the soft interior bread from the top half, leaving a shell about ¾ inch (2 cm) thick. This creates a bowl for the olive salad so the sandwich sits flat instead of bulging, and it reduces the total amount of bread relative to filling. Save the torn-out bread for breadcrumbs.

instructions.title: Toast the cut faces
instructions.text: Brush both cut surfaces with 2 tbsp of the oil that has pooled at the top of the olive salad, then toast them cut side up on a sheet pan at 400°F (205°C) for 6 to 8 minutes until lightly golden. Toasting builds a barrier so that hours of oil contact soften the bread pleasantly instead of dissolving it. Let the halves cool completely before you build.

instructions.title: Spread olive salad on both halves
instructions.text: Spoon about 1 cup (240 ml) of drained olive salad into the hollowed top half and another ½ cup (120 ml) onto the bottom half, pressing it into an even layer. Let the excess oil drain off the spoon first — you want the flavor and the texture, not a puddle. Both halves get salad so every bite carries it.

instructions.title: Layer the meats and cheese
instructions.text: On the bottom half, layer in this order: provolone, salami, mortadella, capicola, then mozzarella. Cheese on the outside of the meat stack, top and bottom, insulates the bread from the oily cured meats. Lay each slice flat and overlapping rather than folded, so the sandwich compresses into even layers.

instructions.title: Close and wrap tightly
instructions.text: Set the top half on, press down firmly with both palms, and wrap the entire loaf tightly in plastic wrap, then again in foil. The wrapping is what holds everything in place during pressing. Wrap it snugly enough that the sandwich holds its shape when you pick it up.

instructions.title: Press under weight
instructions.text: Set the wrapped loaf on a sheet pan, lay a second sheet pan on top, and weigh it down with a cast-iron skillet or a few cans, about 5 lb (2.3 kg) total. Refrigerate and press for at least 2 hours and ideally 8 hours or overnight. Pressing drives the olive oil into the bread and compacts the layers into something you can actually bite through.

instructions.title: Rest at room temperature
instructions.text: Take the sandwich out of the fridge 30 minutes before serving and leave it wrapped. Cold cured meat tastes flat and cold provolone is waxy, while at room temperature both come alive. This half hour genuinely changes how the sandwich tastes.

instructions.title: Cut into wedges
instructions.text: Unwrap and cut the loaf into 6 wedges with a serrated knife, using long sawing strokes and cutting all the way through in one pass. Wipe the blade between cuts so the olive salad does not smear across the layers. Serve at room temperature with the extra olive salad on the side.

tips: The olive salad is the soul of this sandwich and keeps 2 weeks refrigerated under a film of oil. Make a double batch and use it on eggs, pasta, and grilled fish.
If you can only find one kind of cured meat, choose Genoa salami and use 1 lb of it. A muffuletta with only salami is far better than one with three mediocre meats.
Pressing overnight is genuinely better than 2 hours. Build it after dinner and you have lunch for the next two days already made.
Wrapped tightly, a pressed muffuletta keeps 3 days in the fridge and travels beautifully, which is why it is the greatest picnic sandwich ever devised.
For a warm version, unwrap and bake the pressed loaf at 350°F (175°C) for 12 minutes before cutting, just until the cheese softens.
recipes.keyTemp: No cooking temperature applies — the sandwich is done when it has pressed down to about two-thirds of its original height and the bread is saturated with olive oil at the seams. Serve at room temperature, roughly 68°F (20°C).
recipes.pairing: Zapp's potato chips, an ice-cold Abita amber, and a wedge of the sandwich for tomorrow.

recipes.title: Slow-Roasted Pulled Pork Sandwiches
recipes.blurb: A whole pork shoulder rubbed the night before and roasted until it collapses, dressed with tangy vinegar sauce and piled onto a soft bun with slaw. Almost all of the eight hours is waiting.

items: 6 lb (2.7 kg) bone-in pork shoulder, also sold as pork butt
2 tsp (5 g) freshly ground black pepper
1 tbsp (15 ml) yellow mustard, as a binder
1 cup (240 ml) water, for the roasting pan
½ tsp (1 g) freshly ground black pepper
3 cups (300 g) crunchy vinegar coleslaw, well drained

instructions.title: Rub the pork a day ahead
instructions.text: Pat the shoulder dry, smear it all over with the 1 tbsp of yellow mustard, then mix the brown sugar, 2 tbsp salt, smoked paprika, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, mustard powder, and cayenne and press that rub into every surface. The mustard is a binder only — you will not taste it. Wrap and refrigerate overnight, which lets the salt penetrate deep into a very thick cut.

instructions.title: Temper before roasting
instructions.text: Take the pork out of the fridge 1 hour before cooking and set it fat side up on a rack in a roasting pan. A 6-pound roast straight from the fridge takes an extra hour just to shake off the chill. Do not trim the fat cap below about ¼ inch (6 mm), since it bastes the meat for the entire cook.

instructions.title: Roast low and steady
instructions.text: Roast at 275°F (135°C) with a rack in the lower third of the oven. Pour 1 cup (240 ml) of water into the pan below the rack to keep the drippings from scorching and to add humidity. Plan on roughly 1 hour 20 minutes per pound, which is a full 8 hours for a 6-pound shoulder, and treat that as an estimate rather than a promise — the thermometer decides when it is done, not the clock.

instructions.title: Expect the stall
instructions.text: Somewhere around 160°F (71°C) the internal temperature will stop climbing for an hour or more. This is the stall, caused by evaporative cooling from the surface, and it is completely normal. Do not raise the oven temperature in a panic; just wait it out or wrap the roast in foil to push through faster.

instructions.title: Make the vinegar sauce
instructions.text: While the pork cooks, whisk the cider vinegar, 2 tbsp brown sugar, ketchup, 1 tsp salt, red pepper flakes, and black pepper in a jar until the sugar dissolves. Let it sit at room temperature for at least an hour so the pepper flakes infuse. This thin Carolina-style sauce is a seasoning, not a glaze — it is there to cut the richness of the pork, not to coat it.

instructions.title: Cook to 203°F
instructions.text: The pork is ready when an instant-read thermometer slides into the thickest part with no resistance, right around 203°F (95°C). Whole pork is safe at 145°F (63°C), but shoulder needs to go this much higher for the collagen to melt into gelatin and the meat to pull apart. Start probing at the 6-hour mark and check in a few different spots.

instructions.title: Rest it long
instructions.text: Tent the roast loosely with foil and rest it for a full hour before touching it. This is the longest rest in this whole book and it is worth every minute; the gelatin and juices need time to settle back into the muscle. Pulling it hot means a puddle on the board and dry pork in the bun.

instructions.title: Pull, do not shred to death
instructions.text: Pull the bone straight out — it should slide free with almost no effort — then pull the meat apart with two forks or gloved hands into rough, irregular strands. Leave some pieces chunky rather than reducing everything to fluff, because texture variation is what makes it interesting. Discard any large pockets of unrendered fat but keep the darker bark bits mixed in.

instructions.title: Dress the meat
instructions.text: Pour about ¾ cup (180 ml) of the vinegar sauce over the pulled pork along with ½ cup (120 ml) of the defatted pan drippings and toss to combine. Taste and add more sauce a splash at a time until it tastes bright and seasoned rather than merely rich. Keep the remaining sauce on the table.

instructions.title: Butter and toast the buns
instructions.text: Spread the softened butter on the cut faces and toast them in a skillet over medium heat for about 60 seconds until golden. Soft potato buns are the correct choice — they compress around the filling instead of pushing it out the sides the way a crusty roll does. The toasted face is your only defense against the vinegar sauce.

instructions.title: Build with slaw on top
instructions.text: Lay pickle chips on the bottom bun, pile on about 5 oz (140 g) of pulled pork, then finish with a generous handful of well-drained slaw and the top bun. Slaw goes on top so its dressing does not soak down through the pork into the bread, and its cold crunch is a deliberate contrast to the soft, hot meat. Press gently and serve immediately.

tips: Pulled pork keeps 4 days refrigerated and 3 months frozen. Reheat it in a covered pan with a splash of cider vinegar and stock so it steams back to life instead of drying out.
Drain your coleslaw in a sieve for 10 minutes before it goes on the sandwich. Undrained slaw is the fastest way to destroy a good bun.
A slow cooker works if the oven is spoken for: 8 to 10 hours on low, then spread the pulled meat on a sheet pan and broil for 5 minutes to get some bark back.
Save the defatted pan drippings. That cup of concentrated pork jus is the best thing you can add back to the meat and most people throw it away.
Bone-in beats boneless every time. The bone conducts heat toward the center, adds gelatin, and gives you an unmistakable doneness test when it pulls clean.
recipes.keyTemp: Whole pork is safe at 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest, but shoulder must reach about 203°F (95°C) for the connective tissue to break down and the meat to pull.
recipes.pairing: Baked beans, cornbread, and an ice-cold cider or a hoppy pale ale.

recipes.title: Triple-Decker Turkey Club
recipes.blurb: Three slices of toast, two fillings, and four frilled picks holding the whole architectural achievement together. It is a diner classic because the layering genuinely works.

items: 6 slices good white sandwich bread, ½ in (1 cm) thick
8 oz (225 g) thinly sliced roast turkey breast
4 large leaves crisp romaine or iceberg lettuce
2 medium ripe tomatoes (about 12 oz / 340 g), cut into 8 slices ¼ in (6 mm) thick
½ tsp (2 g) flaky sea salt
¼ tsp (1 g) freshly ground black pepper
8 frilled sandwich picks or long toothpicks

instructions.title: Bake the bacon flat
instructions.text: Lay the bacon in a single layer on a foil-lined sheet pan, put it in a cold oven, and set the temperature to 400°F (205°C). Bake 16 to 20 minutes until deep brown and just barely flexible. Flat oven bacon is essential in a triple-decker, because curled slices create air gaps that make the tower unstable and impossible to cut cleanly.

instructions.title: Salt and drain the tomato
instructions.text: Lay all 8 tomato slices on paper towels, season with ¼ tsp of the flaky salt, and let them drain 10 minutes while the bacon cooks. Blot the tops before using. A club has two layers of filling and twice the opportunity to go soggy, so drying the tomato matters even more here than in a BLT.

instructions.title: Crisp the lettuce
instructions.text: Soak the lettuce leaves in ice water for 5 minutes, then dry them completely in a salad spinner or between towels. Tear or trim them so they sit within the footprint of the bread rather than hanging over the edges. Overhanging lettuce is what makes a club fall apart when you cut it.

instructions.title: Toast all six slices
instructions.text: Toast the bread until firm and evenly golden, about 3 minutes in a toaster. Every slice must be properly toasted, including the middle one, since that center slice is the structural beam holding two separate sandwiches together. A soft middle slice collapses under the weight and the whole thing slides sideways.

instructions.title: Mayonnaise every inside face
instructions.text: Spread mayonnaise on one face of the top and bottom slices and on both faces of the middle slice, using about 1 tbsp per surface and going right to the crust. That is four mayonnaised surfaces per sandwich and eight across the two, which is exactly what the ½ cup covers. Beyond flavor, the mayo is a fat barrier that keeps moisture from wicking into the toast, so a bare corner is a corner that goes soggy first.

instructions.title: Build the bottom layer
instructions.text: On the bottom slice, lay down lettuce first, then half the turkey folded into loose ruffles rather than laid flat, then 2 tomato slices seasoned with salt and pepper. Ruffling the turkey traps air and gives the sandwich height and a better bite than a compressed slab. Lettuce on the bottom keeps tomato juice off the toast.

instructions.title: Add the middle slice
instructions.text: Set the double-mayonnaised middle slice on top and press down gently to settle the first layer. Make sure it is aligned squarely with the bottom slice, because a crooked middle slice guarantees a leaning tower. This is the moment to check that nothing is hanging over the edges.

instructions.title: Build the second layer
instructions.text: On the middle slice, layer the bacon first, broken into halves and crosshatched to cover the surface evenly, then the remaining turkey, then the last 2 tomato slices and more lettuce. Putting bacon directly against the dry middle toast keeps the salty fat where it can season everything. Finish with the top slice, mayonnaise side down.

instructions.title: Pin it before you cut
instructions.text: Press the whole stack down firmly with your palm for 5 seconds, then push a sandwich pick vertically through the center of each of the four quadrants, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) in from each corner. The picks are not decoration; they are the only thing keeping a five-inch tall sandwich together while a knife goes through it. Push them all the way to the bottom slice.

instructions.title: Cut into four triangles
instructions.text: With a long serrated knife, cut the sandwich corner to corner in both directions to make 4 triangles, sawing gently rather than pressing down. Wipe the blade between the two cuts for clean edges. Serve immediately with chips and a pickle, arranging the triangles points up the way a diner would.

tips: Roast your own turkey breast if you have the time, or ask the deli to slice it thick, about ⅛ inch (3 mm). Paper-thin deli turkey packs into a wet, flavorless mat.
Add a thin layer of sliced avocado in the bottom layer for a California club, or swap the mayo for herbed mayonnaise with 1 tbsp of chopped tarragon.
Bacon can be cooked 3 days ahead and recrisped for 4 minutes at 350°F (175°C), which turns this into a genuinely fast lunch.
If the sandwich is too tall to bite, that is normal. Cutting into quarters rather than halves is exactly why the club is traditionally served in triangles.
Use a bread with a tight crumb. Airy bakery bread compresses unevenly and the tower will lean before you get a knife into it.
recipes.keyTemp: Deli turkey is already cooked and served cold here; if you roast your own breast, cook it to 165°F (74°C) and chill it fully before slicing.
recipes.pairing: Kettle chips, a dill pickle spear, and iced tea or a crisp lager.
